ai.definition: De novo protein design involves creating entirely new proteins from scratch that have desired properties and functions. This technology is used in synthetic biology to develop proteins tailored for specific applications.
ai.howItWorks: The process starts with computational modeling and simulation to predict the structure of a protein based on its amino acid sequence. Once designed, the protein's DNA sequence is synthesized and expressed using genetic engineering techniques. The resulting protein can then be tested for its desired function.
ai.problemSolved: Climate change and environmental pollution, particularly carbon capture and plastic degradation.
ai.manufacturing: The manufacturing process involves several steps: design, synthesis of DNA, transformation into host cells, expression, purification, and testing of the designed proteins.
ai.buildProcess: Involves computational modeling to predict protein structures, followed by laboratory work for gene synthesis, cell transformation, and protein production.
ai.costDrivers: High initial investment in computational tools, high costs associated with DNA synthesis and protein expression, and extensive validation steps required to ensure the protein functions as designed.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The technology is expected to progress from lab-scale experiments to pilot studies and eventually commercial applications as it matures.
ai.regulation: Currently, there are no specific regulations for de novo protein design. However, environmental safety and biosafety considerations will likely drive regulatory frameworks in the future.
ai.risks: Environmental risks such as unintended release of engineered organisms into the environment, ethical concerns related to synthetic biology, and potential misuse of the technology.
ai.profitability: Potential for significant economic benefits if successful, but high initial costs and uncertain market demand pose challenges.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future developments may include advancements in computational tools, more efficient synthesis methods, and improved understanding of protein function and design principles.

glossary.def: The process of creating entirely new proteins from scratch with specific desired functions.
A field that uses engineering principles to design and construct new biological parts, devices, and systems.

subsystems.name: Generative design engine
subsystems.role: invents new protein backbones and sequences that do not exist in nature.

subsystems.name: Active-site and binding spec
subsystems.role: defines what the protein must do: which molecule it grabs or splits, and where.

subsystems.name: Expression host
subsystems.role: the cell factory that actually makes the designed protein.

subsystems.name: Screening and assay
subsystems.role: tests thousands of designs for real activity, not just predicted shape.

subsystems.name: Stability engineering
subsystems.role: makes the protein survive heat, salt, solvents or extreme pH.

subsystems.name: Immobilisation and contactor
subsystems.role: fixes the enzyme so it can be reused in an industrial column or reactor.

subsystems.name: Downstream product handling
subsystems.role: deals with what the enzyme makes.

buildSteps.title: Pick the reaction
buildSteps.detail: Choose a target chemistry — splitting a plastic polymer, hydrating CO2 to bicarbonate, or oxidising methane — and the conditions it must work in.

buildSteps.title: Specify the fold and active site
buildSteps.detail: Decide the geometry: where the catalytic residues sit and how the substrate binds.

buildSteps.title: Generate candidate backbones
buildSteps.detail: Diffusion models such as RFdiffusion propose thousands of new protein scaffolds that already hold the active site in the right shape.

buildSteps.title: Design sequences
buildSteps.detail: An inverse-folding model fills each backbone with amino acids that will fold into it and pack stably.

buildSteps.title: Filter by prediction
buildSteps.detail: AlphaFold-style predictors and physics scoring throw out designs whose predicted structure or energy does not match the intent.

buildSteps.title: Make the proteins
buildSteps.detail: Synthesise the DNA, clone it into a host, and express and purify the proteins.

buildSteps.title: Measure real activity
buildSteps.detail: Assay the designs against the target substrate and keep the few that work better than chance.

buildSteps.title: Evolve and stabilise
buildSteps.detail: Round after round of mutation, selection and machine-learning guidance raises activity, then thermostability and solvent tolerance.

buildSteps.title: Immobilise and scale
buildSteps.detail: Bind or entrap the best variants on a support and fit them into a reactor or capture contactor, then test at pilot scale.

prerequisites.why: design depends on knowing what a sequence will actually fold into; AlphaFold2 in 2020 made this routine.
RFdiffusion and similar models design new folds, but hit rates on hard chemistries remain low.

prerequisites.tech: Cheap, fast DNA synthesis and high-throughput screening
prerequisites.why: you must build and test thousands of designs to find one that works.
natural enzymes often denature in hot, salty or solvent-laden process streams.
reusable, stable biocatalysts are needed to make the economics work outside the lab.

pathway.milestone: designed binders and simple catalysts proven in the lab, plus engineered PET-degrading enzymes such as FAST-PETase
pathway.unlocks: confidence that de novo design can produce working, useful proteins.

pathway.milestone: designed enzymes for plastic depolymerisation reaching pilot recycling plants
pathway.unlocks: a route to recycle mixed or coloured plastics that mechanical recycling rejects.

pathway.milestone: carbonic-anhydrase-based CO2 capture tested in industrial flue-gas streams
pathway.unlocks: lower-energy capture of CO2 from cement, steel and power plants.

pathway.milestone: biocatalysts for methane oxidation and other hard reactions at scale
pathway.unlocks: new routes to turn waste carbon into fuels and chemicals.
